people.name: The Storyteller
people.summary: The elder who holds the band's memory.
people.intro: He is the oldest man in the band and its memory. He knows every story, every safe path, and every good tide. He cannot walk far now, but the band still turns to him, and he still has things to give.

facets.description_1: At first light he walks to the edge of the cliff and stands alone above the sea. He comes here every morning. He says that he comes to look at the water, but the others know that he comes to remember: every story he has told, and every person who was in them.
facets.description_2: Among hunter-gatherer peoples studied in recent times, the elders hold knowledge that no one else has: where to find water in a drought that comes once in a lifetime, which plants heal, and which stories hold the group's history. When an elder dies, that knowledge is lost unless someone has learned it.
facets.alt: Oil painting of an elderly African man with short white curly hair and a white beard, in a hide cloak and a string of white shell beads, standing on a cliff at dawn with both hands on a wooden staff, looking out over the sea.

facets.description_1: At low tide he sits on a flat rock and calls the children to him. He holds up a mussel and shows them which ones are good to take, which pools are safe, and when the sea will turn. His leg keeps him from the far rocks now, so he makes sure that the children know them.
facets.description_2: At Pinnacle Point in South Africa, people gathered shellfish about 164,000 years ago. Archaeologists think that they timed their visits to the lowest tides, which follow the cycle of the moon. Knowing when and where to gather was knowledge that passed from the old to the young.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the elderly man sitting on a rock at low tide, holding up a black mussel and pointing to a cluster of mussels while three children watch, with a cave in a sandstone cliff behind them.

facets.description_1: Each morning the band walks away along the shore to gather food, and he stays behind at the shelter. The old wound on his leg has never fully healed. He watches them go until they are small dots on the sand. Then someone at the back always turns and waves.
facets.description_2: At Romito Cave in Italy, a young man buried about 11,000 years ago had a form of dwarfism that limited how he could move and work. He lived to adulthood because his group cared for him. Skeletons from many Stone Age sites show injuries that healed over many years in the same way.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the elderly man sitting at the mouth of a cliff-top cave shelter beside cold ashes, watching a small group of people walk away along a long beach far below, one child waving back.

facets.description_1: One evening by the fire, a little girl climbs onto his knee and tells him a story of her own. She lifts her hands high, the way he does, and makes up the words as she goes. He laughs until his eyes close. No story he has ever told has made him this happy.
facets.description_2: In Rouffignac Cave in France, children as young as three drew lines with their fingers in the soft clay of the cave walls. Some marks are so high that an adult must have lifted the child up to make them. Play and learning were part of the same life.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the elderly man laughing by a fire with a little girl in a hide tunic on his knee, her hands raised as she tells a story, with hand stencils on the cave wall and two smiling adults behind.

facets.description_1: At sunset he sits on the cliff with the friend he has known all his life. They were boys together on these rocks. Now they sit side by side and say nothing at all. His friend's hand rests on his back. The man who tells every story needs no words here.
facets.description_2: Among the Ju/'hoan people of the Kalahari, a gift-exchange partnership called hxaro can last a whole lifetime and tie families together across long distances. Ostrich eggshell beads, the kind of gift that hxaro partners still give, travelled thousands of kilometres across Africa between 50,000 and 33,000 years ago.
facets.alt: Oil painting of two elderly men sitting side by side on a cliff at sunset above the sea, one with white curly hair and a staff, the other bald, his hand resting on his friend's back.

facets.description_1: Tonight a young woman tells the story by the fire. She lifts her hands high, as he taught her, and the children lean in to listen. He sits at the edge of the light, where no one looks at him. That is how he wanted it. The stories no longer need him to live.
facets.description_2: In a study of Ju/'hoan conversations, anthropologist Polly Wiessner found that daytime talk was mostly about work and complaints. At night around the fire, most of the talk was stories: about people, places, and the past. Firelight, she argued, gave humans the time to pass on what they knew.
facets.alt: Oil painting of a young woman by a fire in a cave raising both hands as she tells a story to children in hide tunics, her hand shadows on a wall of hand stencils, while the elderly man watches from the edge of the light.

people.name: The Grandmother
people.summary: The elder who carries the band through winter.
people.intro: She is the oldest woman of the Ice Age band. She has lived through more winters than anyone else, and she remembers every one. Her hands have sewn the coats that keep the band warm, and her memory holds the paths that lead them to safety.

facets.description_1: Late at night, when the others sleep, she sits by the stone lamp and threads a needle. Her eyes are not as sharp as they were, so she holds the needle close to the flame. She has done this every winter night for fifty years.
facets.description_2: Bone needles with an eye, like the one she uses, appear at Ice Age sites across Europe and Asia. Some of the oldest are more than 40,000 years old. With them, people could sew fitted clothes from fur and hide.
facets.alt: Oil painting of an elderly Ice Age woman with long white hair, in a fur parka and a necklace of ivory beads with a fox tooth, threading a bone needle by the light of a stone lamp in a dark cave, a charcoal horse faint on the wall.

facets.description_1: By day, at the mouth of the cave, she fits a new parka on a little boy and checks each seam at his shoulder. A young woman kneels beside her and watches every stitch. One day she will sew the coats, and she must learn now.
facets.description_2: Body lice live only in clothing. Genetic studies show that they split from head lice at least 83,000 years ago. This suggests that people have worn clothing at least that long, and fitted clothing let them survive the cold.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the elderly woman kneeling at a snowy cave mouth, sewing a fur parka on a small boy with a bone needle, while a young woman with braids holds sinew thread and watches, with bone needles and a flint flake on a stone.

facets.description_1: It is the hardest winter she can remember. Snow blocks the door, and the fire is almost out. She has one strip of dried meat left. She gives it to her granddaughter and nods, as if she has already eaten.
facets.description_2: At Ice Age camps on the plains of Ukraine and Russia, people dug storage pits into the frozen ground to keep meat for the winter. In a long winter, the stores could run out before spring.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the elderly woman inside a mammoth-bone shelter at night, holding out a strip of dried meat to a young girl wrapped in fur, an empty stone on her lap, low embers, sleeping family behind, and snow at a doorway framed by tusks.

facets.description_1: The first warm day of spring. She sits in the sun outside the bone house with her eyes closed and her hands open to the warmth. Around her, the children she kept alive all winter run through the first flowers.
facets.description_2: The teeth of reindeer from Ice Age camps in France show the season in which each animal died. From them, archaeologists can see that people moved with the seasons and the herds.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the elderly woman sitting on a fur outside a hide-covered shelter in spring, face turned up to the sun with eyes closed and hands open, while four children in hide tunics run through yellow flowers, with a stream and reindeer behind.

facets.description_1: By the fire, her grown daughter braids her long white hair, the way she once braided her daughter's. Something one of them says sets them both laughing, while the baby sleeps beside them.
facets.description_2: Small Ice Age carvings show that hair mattered. The ivory head from Brassempouy in France, about 25,000 years old, shows a woman's hair arranged in a careful grid pattern.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the elderly woman laughing with a hand over her mouth while her adult daughter braids her long white hair by a fire, a baby asleep in fur beside them, horse paintings on the cave wall and a stone lamp on a ledge.

facets.description_1: She leads the young people over the high pass, the way her own grandmother once led her. At the stone marker she stops and points to the sheltered valley below. One day, one of them will stand here and point for someone else.
facets.description_2: Shells from the Mediterranean and the Atlantic coasts appear at Ice Age sites in central Europe, hundreds of kilometres from the sea. People travelled, traded, and passed on the knowledge of routes across great distances.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the elderly woman in a fur hood standing beside a stack of stones at a snowy mountain pass, pointing down to a river valley with reindeer, while five young people carrying hide bundles climb toward her.

people.name: The Bead-Maker
people.summary: The woman whose gifts keep the peace.
people.intro: She makes the band's beads, and every string she makes is a gift. Her necklaces bind friends together, welcome strangers, and carry her band's name to places far away. She is the band's peacemaker, and she does it with her hands.

facets.description_1: At sunset she walks the tideline with her pouch at her waist. She picks up each small shell, holds it up to the light, and turns it in her fingers. Only the best are good enough to become beads.
facets.description_2: The shell beads from Blombos Cave in South Africa, about 75,000 years old, were made from one kind of small sea snail. The makers chose shells of a similar size and pierced each one in the same place.
facets.alt: Oil painting of an African woman with her curly hair in a high bun and strings of white and red shell beads, standing at the edge of the sea at sunset, holding a small shell up to the light, with a leather pouch at her waist.

facets.description_1: In the shelter, she pierces shell after shell with her bone awl and colours some of them red with ochre. Her bag fills with necklaces. They are not only beautiful: they are the gifts that keep her band at peace with its neighbours.
facets.description_2: At Blombos Cave, people mixed ground red ochre in abalone shells about 100,000 years ago, the oldest known paint workshop in the world. Some of the shell beads from the same cave carry traces of ochre.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the woman sitting cross-legged in a rock shelter, piercing a tiny shell with a bone awl, with raw shells, a lump of red ochre, a grinding stone, red-stained shells, and finished necklaces spilling from a bag in front of her.

facets.description_1: At the river crossing, her band meets strangers. No one moves. Then she walks out alone onto the stones and holds out her finest necklace. On the far bank, an old woman takes the first step toward her.
facets.description_2: At Olorgesailie in Kenya, people about 300,000 years ago used black obsidian brought from 25 to 95 kilometres away. Exchange across such distances needed peaceful meetings between groups who did not live together.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the woman standing alone on stepping stones in a river, holding out a necklace toward a group of strangers with white clay lines on their skin, while an older stranger steps toward her and her own band waits on the other bank.

facets.description_1: At a gathering on the beach, the drum starts, and she pulls the man she loves into the circle. They spin by the fire, laughing, her beads swinging out in the firelight. He wears a string of them too.
facets.description_2: Rock paintings in southern Africa, made by San artists over thousands of years, show people dancing in circles while others clap. Among San communities today, the dance around a night fire is still a central event of community life.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the woman and a man laughing and spinning hand in hand by a fire on a beach at night, her bead necklaces swinging, while others clap, a man beats a log drum, an older woman sways, and two children dance.

facets.description_1: Once a year the bands gather by the river, and she finds her older sister, who married into another band. They trade necklaces, then hold each other's faces, foreheads together, and cry.
facets.description_2: At Enkapune Ya Muto in Kenya, people made beads from ostrich eggshell about 50,000 years ago, among the oldest of their kind. Among the Ju/'hoan of the Kalahari, gifts of such beads still tie families together across distant bands.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the woman and her older sister, who has white clay lines on her face, holding each other's faces with foreheads touching and tears of joy, both wearing new necklaces, at a large gathering by a river with fires and shelters.

facets.description_1: At dawn, a young woman leaves to join a distant band. The Bead-Maker folds her finest necklace into the young woman's hands. Her beads will travel to places she will never see.
facets.description_2: At Taforalt Cave in Morocco, archaeologists found shell beads about 82,000 years old, more than 40 kilometres from the sea where the shells were collected. Beads travelled farther than the people who made them.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the woman placing a long shell-bead necklace into the hands of a tearful young woman with a bundle on her back, at dawn beside a sandstone overhang with a fire, while three travellers wait on a path leading inland.

people.name: The Flute Player
people.summary: The father who makes the band's music.
people.intro: He is the band's musician. He carves flutes from the wing bones of birds, and he plays for every moment that matters: the long winter nights, the dead, the newly born, and the joy of spring. His wife is the Painter. Between them, the band's caves are full of pictures and song.

facets.description_1: At dusk he climbs alone to the ridge above the frozen valley and plays. No one asked him to. He plays because the valley is quiet and the sky is wide, and his breath steams in the cold with every note.
facets.description_2: In Hohle Fels Cave in Germany, archaeologists found a flute made from the wing bone of a griffon vulture, about 40,000 years old. It has five finger holes and a V-shaped notch for the mouth. It is one of the oldest known musical instruments in the world.
facets.alt: Oil painting of an Ice Age man in a fur parka standing on a snowy ridge at dusk, playing a pale bone flute with his eyes closed, his breath steaming, above a frozen river valley under a deep blue sky with a rose-coloured horizon.

facets.description_1: At the mouth of the cave, he cuts the last hole in a new flute made from a swan's wing bone and blows the first note. He listens like a judge. Beside him, a boy stares as if a bone has just learned to sing.
facets.description_2: At Geissenklösterle Cave in Germany, a flute made from a swan's wing bone is about 42,000 years old. Another flute from the same cave was carved from mammoth ivory, a far harder task that needed great skill.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the man sitting on a fur at a snowy cave mouth, testing a new bone flute while an amazed boy in a fur parka watches, with a swan wing, a feather, flint tools, bone shavings, and an older flute on the hide in front of them.

facets.description_1: On a grey winter morning, the band buries a friend. He stands at the grave with tears on his face and plays the slowest song he knows, while the others lay their gifts on the covered body.
facets.description_2: At Sungir in Russia, about 34,000 years ago, people buried a man and two children with thousands of ivory beads and carved ivory animals, including a small horse. The care in these burials shows how deeply they mourned their dead.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the man playing a bone flute with his eyes closed beside a shallow grave in the snow, where a covered body lies with a string of ivory beads and a carved ivory horse, while a woman kneels and the band and two children stand in grief.

facets.description_1: Deep in the cave, he plays one note, and the whole chamber sings it back. The band stops still with their lamps raised. The children laugh. He has found the place where the stone itself makes music.
facets.description_2: In French caves such as Arcy-sur-Cure, researcher Iégor Reznikoff found that many painted dots and figures sit at the places where the cave resonates most strongly. The first artists may have chosen their walls by listening.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the man playing a bone flute in a high cave chamber with stalactites, red dots, and a painted mammoth on the walls, surrounded by members of his band holding small stone lamps and two laughing children, all looking up in wonder.

facets.description_1: Late at night, his wife paints a horse on the cave wall by the light of one small lamp. He sits behind her and plays softly, and he does not look at his flute. He watches her.
facets.description_2: In Hohle Fels Cave, the vulture-bone flute was found close to one of the oldest carved human figures in the world, the Venus of Hohle Fels. Music and art were made by the same people, in the same places.
facets.alt: Oil painting of a woman with dark braids drawing a horse in charcoal on a cave wall covered with older animal paintings, while the man sits behind her playing a bone flute, with a stone lamp, charcoal sticks, and a shell of red ochre on a rock between them.

facets.description_1: By the fire, he gives the children small flutes that he carved for them. Not one note is in tune. He laughs louder than anyone and keeps the beat, because this is how every musician begins.
facets.description_2: The flutes from the caves of southern Germany span several thousand years and were made from different bones and from ivory. The skill of making and playing them passed from one generation to the next.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the man laughing as he leads five children in fur parkas who blow small bone flutes by a fire in a cave, while adults behind them smile and one covers her ears, with painted horses and a mammoth on the wall.

people.name: The Painter
people.summary: The mother who gives the band its pictures.
people.intro: She paints the animals that the band lives among: horses, bison, the great wild ox. She grinds her own colours, crawls into the deepest parts of the cave, and works by the light of one small flame. Her husband is the Flute Player, and her daughter is learning to paint beside her.

facets.description_1: Deep in the cave, she stands beside the horse she has just finished, red ochre still on her fingers. She holds the lamp low and looks at the work for a long time. Tomorrow she will start the next one.
facets.description_2: In Chauvet Cave in France, painters drew horses, lions, and rhinoceroses in charcoal and ochre about 36,000 years ago. They are among the oldest and most skilled cave paintings ever found.
facets.alt: Oil painting of an Ice Age woman with two dark braids and a smudge of red ochre on her cheek, standing in a dark cave beside a horse painted on the wall, one red-stained hand on the rock and a small stone lamp in the other.

facets.description_1: At the mouth of the cave, she grinds red ochre on a flat stone and lays out her colours in a row, from pale yellow to black. Every animal on the walls begins here, as powder and patience.
facets.description_2: Ice Age painters made red and yellow from ochre, an earth rich in iron, and black from charcoal and manganese. Some heated yellow ochre in the fire to turn it red, and mixed minerals to make new shades.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the woman kneeling at a cave mouth, grinding red ochre on a flat stone with a round hand stone, with small heaps of yellow, orange, red, and black pigment, lumps of ochre, charcoal sticks, and a shell of paint in front of her.

facets.description_1: The walls she must paint lie far inside the mountain. To reach them, she crawls on her elbows through a passage so low that the rock touches her back, pushing her small lamp ahead of her. If the flame goes out, there is no light at all.
facets.description_2: In Niaux Cave in France, the great panel of bison and horses known as the Salon Noir lies about 800 metres from the entrance, reached through long, dark passages. The painters chose the deepest places on purpose.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the woman in a hooded fur parka crawling through a narrow, low cave passage, her tense face lit from below by a small stone lamp on the rock floor in front of her, surrounded by darkness.

facets.description_1: By lamplight she sees it: a bulge in the wall with the exact shape of a bison's back. She adds a head, horns, and legs with a few lines of charcoal, and the animal steps out of the rock. She laughs out loud.
facets.description_2: In Altamira Cave in Spain, about 15,000 years ago, painters used natural bulges in the ceiling as the bodies of bison. The rock gave the shape, and the painter gave it life.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the woman laughing as she draws the head and legs of a bison onto a natural bulge in the cave wall that forms its body, holding a lit stone lamp low so its light rakes across the rock.

facets.description_1: High on a ladder, she paints a great red wild ox across the ceiling. Below, her closest friend holds the ladder steady and the lamp high, and they laugh at something only the two of them understand.
facets.description_2: At Lascaux Cave in France, about 17,000 years ago, holes cut into the walls of one gallery show that people built scaffolding to reach and paint the high ceilings. Work like that needed more than one pair of hands.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the woman standing on a rough wooden ladder, painting a red aurochs among black horses on a cave ceiling, while her friend with bone pins in her hair holds the ladder and raises a stone lamp, both smiling.

facets.description_1: Years after her daughter's first handprint, she kneels behind the child and guides her small hand along the wall. Together they draw one curving line: the back of a horse, the child's first.
facets.description_2: In Gargas Cave in France, some hand stencils are so small that they belong to young children. Ice Age art was not only made by experts. Children were there, learning, and leaving their own marks.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the woman kneeling behind her young daughter in a cave, guiding the child's hand to draw the first charcoal line of a horse beside two small red handprints, with a finished horse above them and a stone lamp on the floor.

people.name: The Fire-Carrier
people.summary: The young woman who keeps the band's fire alive.
people.intro: She carries the band's fire. Through snow, rain, and long journeys, she keeps the embers alive in a small bark container, because without fire the band cannot survive the winter. Her grandmother taught her, and one day she will teach someone else.

facets.description_1: At dawn she kneels in the snow, opens her bark container, and blows softly on the embers that she carried through the night. They glow, and she breathes again.
facets.description_2: Some foraging peoples studied in recent times, such as the Andaman Islanders, did not make fire at all. They carried glowing embers from camp to camp and guarded them carefully, because a lost fire was hard to replace.
facets.alt: Oil painting of a young Ice Age woman in a hooded fur parka kneeling in the snow at dawn, blowing on glowing embers inside a small birch-bark container held in her hands, with mammoth-bone shelters in the distance.

facets.description_1: Every night, while the band sleeps, she stays awake and feeds the hearth with mammoth bones. No one sees her work. Everyone wakes up warm.
facets.description_2: At Ice Age mammoth-bone camps on the plains of Ukraine and Russia, the hearths are full of burnt bone. Where trees were rare, bone rich in grease was one of the main fuels.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the young woman feeding a mammoth bone into a fire inside a shelter built of mammoth bones and hides at night, while the band sleeps under furs beside the hearth and smoke rises to a hole in the roof.

facets.description_1: A cold rain has killed the embers that she carried for days. Under a dripping rock, with the whole band watching, she strikes flint against pyrite again and again, until one spark catches.
facets.description_2: Flint tools from Neanderthal sites in France, about 50,000 years old, carry wear marks from being struck against pyrite to make sparks. Much later, the Iceman found in the Alps carried dried tinder fungus in his pouch.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the young woman kneeling under a rock overhang in the rain, striking flint against pyrite to send sparks into a nest of dry grass, beside her soaked ember container, while the band huddles behind her under wet furs.

facets.description_1: On a clear winter night, she sits by her small fire and watches the sparks rise, up and up, until they seem to join the lights that flow across the sky.
facets.description_2: Ice Age people watched the sky closely. A carved bone plate from Abri Blanchard in France, about 30,000 years old, carries rows of small marks that some researchers read as a record of the phases of the moon.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the young woman sitting by a small fire in the snow at night, smiling up at sparks that spiral toward green and violet northern lights, with mammoth-bone shelters behind her.

facets.description_1: After a long, cold day of carrying the fire, she sits down by the hearth, worn out. Her grandmother, who taught her to carry fire, wraps her in her own cloak.
facets.description_2: Among the Hadza of Tanzania, grandmothers gather food for their grandchildren, and children with a living grandmother are better fed. Anthropologists call this the grandmother effect, and many think it helped shape the long human life span.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the young woman sitting by a fire with her eyes closed, holding her ember container, while her white-haired grandmother wraps a fur cloak around her shoulders inside a mammoth-bone shelter.

facets.description_1: At the new camp, she opens her bark container and lights a torch for every family from her embers. A line of small flames spreads out across the dark valley.
facets.description_2: Among many foraging peoples, each family keeps its own hearth, and a camp is a circle of fires. Fire passes freely from one hearth to the next, so one fire can light a whole camp.
facets.alt: Oil painting of the young woman lighting a boy's torch from her own at dusk in a snowy river valley, holding her ember container, while families wait with torches and a line of small flames moves away across the plain.
